source_document.body:
Uber Freight’s CEO has publicly come out with the company’s decision to no longer cooperate with Gartner when the technology and management advisory company does future work on the Magic Quadrant designation for Uber Freight.
Gartner’s latest interactions with Uber Freight (NYSE: UBER) over its annual ratings led CEO Rebecca Tinucci to take to LinkedIn and a company blog post to announce the company’s plans to end any cooperative efforts with Gartner on that widely-cited benchmark.
This was Tinucci’s first Gartner review since she became CEO at Uber Freight in August 2025.
In her LInkedIn post, Tinucci said she was “incredibly disappointed by this process and the only thing that’s clear is that this is not somewhere we’ll invest our time going forward. Back to focusing on our customers.”
A little less than a year ago, Gartner had a mixed rating on Uber Freight, putting it below the “cut line” on the “Ability to Execute” Y axis but past the X Axis cut line for the “Completeness of Vision” rating. To be in the Magic Quadrant, a company needs to be above the cut line for both categories, and be in the upper right hand corner of the four-square box: the magic quadrant..
The Magic Quadrant is that part of an X-Y axis box that has “ability to execute” and “completeness of vision” as its two measurements. A company that lands in the Magic Quadrant scores highly on both areas, and companies often tout to their customers, actual and potential, that they ended up in that sought-after space.
The Gartner webpage on its Magic Quadrant says it publishes 176 Magic Quadrant ratings each year.
Emails sent to Gartner had not been responded to by publication time. An Uber Freight spokeswoman declined further comment beyond Tinucci’s comments.
Taking on a giant
Getting into the Magic Quadrant and the ability to wear that as a badge of honor is what makes Tinucci’s public criticism so notable. Potential users of supply chain technology often look to Gartner’s commentary as a guide on what applications it should use. Publicly calling out the Gartner’s processes is a step that not many companies wish to take.
Tinucci wrote that Uber Freight had received its 2026 Fourth Party Logistics Magic Quadrant assessment, and asked for “the evidence behind our backward shift in positioning and consequential cautions.”
“We made it clear our concern was no longer our individual score,” Tinucci wrote. “The review started to feel like a negotiation over the assessment rather than an explanation of the evidence behind it.”
During the review of the score, Tinucci said Uber Freight felt the process was feeling more like a “negotiation” with Gartner (NYSE: IT) “rather than an explanation of the evidence behind it.”
Coming away with little confidence
“Our experience left us without confidence in the standards underpinning the report’s broader comparisons,” Tinucci said.
The company’s participation is presumably not necessary for Gartner to issue a rating. Tinucci said Uber Freight asked Gartner to no longer include its rating in the Magic Quadrant process, but Gartner declined.
“We are sharing our experience so customers and the industry can evaluate the research with that context,” Tinucci wrote.
Gartner does have a rating called Peer Insights. Tinucci said Uber Freight will continue to participate in that process, and she said the company currently has a rating of 4.6 out of 5.
Tinucci offered specifics on what she said were Uber Freight’s criticisms with the Gartner process.
An unidentified analyst from Gartner, according to Tinucci, “contacted our team outside the formal review channel and asked what it would take to get Uber Freight ‘across the finish line.’”
“That analyst raised the possibility of changing scores and removing a caution before Gartner’s authors could explain how they reached the original conclusions,” she wrote.
Trade article an issue
Tinucci said other points made by the Gartner analyst included concern over what the research firm referred to as a “single speculative trade article” as the basis for one negative finding. “When challenged, Gartner proposed materially rewriting it without adequately explaining the basis for the original conclusion or the change,” Tinucci said.
She wrapped up the recap of the process that Uber Freight is objecting to by noting that the “most significant backward movement” in the Gartner rating of Uber Freight was its “Completeness of Vision.” But Tinucci added that “Gartner acknowledged that a reader could find that result difficult to reconcile, that they “probably needed to go back and investigate.”
FourKites had its issues in the past
The sort of public break with Gartner, while rare, is not unprecedented.
In February 2025, supply chain technology leader FourKites said it would withdraw from the Magic Quadrant process. But its withdrawal did not come with the sort of criticism heard from Tinucci.
Instead, FourKites said it was withdrawing because of “the need to prioritize breakthrough AI innovations using Real-time Transportation Visibility Platform that are fundamentally reshaping supply chain operations.”
In a prepared statement released at the time, FourKites described Gartner’s RTTVP models as “not yet (accounting) for our innovation and roadmap.”
Earlier this year, a blog post written by former Gartner analyst Keith Andes , now head of product marketing at EasyVista said of the Magic Quadrant, said this of the benchmark: “I’ve got some wild news for you: the Gartner Magic Quadrant was never intended to tell you which product to buy. It’s not even a product evaluation.”
To stress that point, Andes said Gartner “regularly reminds customers that they are not suggesting everyone buy the leader at the top right of the Magic Quadrant.”
He added that Gartner’s preference is that corporate enterprise software buyers not “default” to that decision.
Instead, Andes wrote, “the Gartner Magic Quadrant is designed to answer one question: How are these vendors performing against each other in the market?”
